**The Weight of Silence and the Lightness of Questions**

I think about silence often. Not the quiet of a library or the hush of early morning before the birds wake, but the deeper, almost suffocating quiet—the kind that settles in when words fail, when explanations crumble, when the only thing left is the weight of what isn’t said. It’s the silence of a room after an argument where both people are too exhausted to speak but too stubborn to admit they’re wrong. It’s the silence between parents and a child who has grown up and left home, the unspoken understanding that time has stretched all the bridges too thin. It’s the silence of a crowd watching the news, realizing that the world has shifted again, and they don’t know how to react.

And yet, silence isn’t always bad. In the early hours of the day, before the demands of the world pull us into their orbit, silence can feel like a sacred thing—a space where thoughts can breathe, where half-formed ideas have room to stretch and grow. I’ve always loved that kind of silence. The kind that surrounds you when you’re reading, or writing, or just staring out a window at nothing in particular. It’s not the absence of sound so much as the absence of noise—of voices competing for attention, of notifications vying for clicks, of the endless hum of everything *needing* something from you.

But too much silence can be paralyzing. I think about the silence of grief—how it can fill a house like a thick fog, pressing against the walls, muffling laughter that should be there but isn’t. How it wraps around your ribs and sits there, heavy and unmoving, until you forget what it’s like to breathe without it. I’ve known that silence. The one that comes after someone you love is gone and the world keeps spinning like nothing’s changed, but for you, the axis has shifted.

I wonder if silence is a language all its own. Not just the pauses between words, but the things we carry without speaking them. The apology left unsaid because pride won’t let it out. The love that’s too afraid to declare itself. The fear that keeps us from asking for what we need. Silence can be a shield, a fortress, or a cage. It can protect or it can suffocate.

And then there’s the converse—the gift of words. The way they can carve space in the silence, make it feel less lonely. A well-timed text from a friend who knows you’re struggling but doesn’t ask you to explain. A poem that captures exactly what you couldn’t say. A stranger’s smile in a crowded room that makes you feel seen. Words, when they’re chosen carefully, can be bridges. But they can also be weapons, accidentally or otherwise.

I’ve spent a lot of time in my life trying to fill silence with words. Talking too much because I’m afraid of the quiet. Explaining myself endlessly because I’m worried the real me won’t be enough. Writing pages of half-baked thoughts because I need to feel like I’m *doing* something, even if it’s just spinning in place. Maybe that’s why I love writing that reflects on silence so much—the way it challenges me to sit with the unknown, to embrace the unanswered instead of rushing to fill it.

There’s a Zen story about a student who asks a master, *"How can I find peace?"* and the master replies, *"Go on with what you’re doing."* The student, frustrated, says, *"But I *know* what I’m doing isn’t bringing me peace."* And the master says, *"Then stop."*

It’s a deceptively simple idea, but there’s a truth in it. Sometimes the silence isn’t something to escape; it’s the thing itself that needs no fixing. Maybe peace isn’t about having the right words or the perfect response. Maybe it’s about learning to exist in the spaces between them.

I think about how we’re all just trying to make sense of things. Of love and loss, of joy and pain, of the way time reshapes us without warning. We cling to patterns, to routines, to the illusion that we’re in control. But life keeps reminding us that we’re not. A sudden illness. A shattered relationship. The death of a dream we didn’t even realize we had. And in those moments, silence is the only honest response.

But maybe honesty isn’t about having all the answers. Maybe it’s about asking better questions. The kind that don’t just seek solutions but acknowledge the mystery of being alive. *"What if I did this?" "Why does this still ache?" "What would happen if I let it?"*

I don’t know if I’ll ever fully understand silence. But I know that when I stop trying to fill it with noise, it becomes something else entirely—a presence rather than an absence. It’s the hum of the refrigerator at night, the rhythm of my own breath, the faint sound of rain on pavement when I’m not expecting it. It’s not the absence of anything. It’s a place where I can just… *be*.

And perhaps that’s the most radical act of all—to exist without explaining, without justifying, without performing. To stand in the quiet and feel the solid ground under your feet, even when the world feels shaky.

So maybe the next time silence feels heavy, I’ll try not to rush. Maybe I’ll let it sit there with me for a while. Because in the end, we’re all just trying to find our way through the noise—even when the noise is the silence we’re afraid to hear.
